en: There is a fishery that everyone shares. If I catch a little more, I keep the gain alone while the cost of depletion is spread over everyone. Does everyone end up ruined, or can mutual monitoring and rules protect it? Follow the debate between Hardin and Ostrom with numbers.

The stock of a shared resource (a fishery or pasture) starts near its capacity of 100 and regrows logistically each round. When the stock is at half (50), the most that can be caught sustainably each round is 10.

Several users decide each round how much to catch. Payoff is the catch minus the cost of effort. There are three strategies: Greedy (catch 3 times the sustainable share), Restrained (catch only the sustainable share) and Conditional cooperator (restrain if at least half of people restrained last round, otherwise be greedy).

With monitoring on, anyone who catches more than the restrained share is caught with some probability and pays a fine equal to a multiple of that round's catch. This stands in for the community monitoring and sanctions Ostrom described.

Payoff is an average of recent payoffs (memory 0.8). Each round, each person has a 25% chance of looking at one random person and copying that person's strategy the more that person earned. With a 1% chance a new strategy appears. At the start 10% are restrained, the conditional cooperators follow the slider, and the rest are greedy.

What it shows: In this setup, with no monitoring the stock collapsed to 1–2% of capacity (the lowest point came at round 22 on average), then partly recovered and settled at an average of about 26% over the final stretch (average of 10 runs, range 18–40%). The catch was about 70% (7.0) of the sustainable maximum of 10. Raising the chance of being caught raised the stock: about 39% at 20% (catch 9.1), about 45% at 50% (catch 9.9), and about 48% at 100% (catch 10.0). Fines mattered too. At a 20% chance of being caught, with fines of 0 or 0.5 times the catch the stock was 28% and 27%, similar to no monitoring, while at 1 times it was 39% and at 3 times 44%. However, even strong monitoring did not prevent the initial collapse. In 20 of 20 runs at every monitoring level tested (0, 30, 60 and 100%) the stock dropped below 10% of capacity at least once, and the average lowest point was about 1.5% with no monitoring and about 5.8% at 100% monitoring. So in this model monitoring did not prevent the initial collapse, but it raised the level at which the stock recovered and stayed.

What it doesn't show: It is not a proof that Hardin or Ostrom is right. The results depend on the numbers this project chose: the cost of effort (25), the regrowth rate (0.4), the strength of greed (3 times the sustainable share), the copying rule, and a structure in which "being greedy does not pay when the stock is low", because of which the stock did not vanish entirely with no monitoring but stayed near the cost, at about 26%. A different structure would give different results. Also, in small groups (10 and 20 users) some runs collapsed all the way to 0, and the share of conditional cooperators did not clearly change the outcome in this setup (22–26% with no monitoring). Real shared resources involve ownership, outsiders' entry, information, trust and the role of the state, and the success stories Ostrom studied are about cases where conditions such as clear boundaries and local rules were in place.

This is this project's own implementation, inspired by the debate between Hardin (1968), "The Tragedy of the Commons", Science 162, and Ostrom (1990), Governing the Commons. The resource part simplifies the fishery economics of Gordon (1954), Journal of Political Economy 62, and Schaefer (1954) (logistic regrowth and catch proportional to effort). It does not reproduce numbers from those works.

Stock capacity 100, regrowth rate 0.4, initial stock 80, cost of effort 25, greed is 3 times the restrained share, copying probability 25% (Fermi rule, a logistic of the payoff difference divided by 0.5), mutation 1%. The numbers above are all averages of 10 runs and change with the settings (node tools/validate-commons.js).
The code is available on GitHub.
Do Nice People Survive? · Simulatio Lab
Do people who trust and cooperate just get betrayed? Run the repeated prisoner's dilemma (a trust game) and see when cooperation spreads or collapses.

Do people who trust others and cooperate just get taken advantage of by betrayers? What happens to trust when a society has many liars and cheaters? Watch people repeat a "trust game" (the repeated prisoner's dilemma), where cooperating together pays but cheating alone pays even more, while copying each other.

240 people each use one of five strategies: Always cooperate, Always defect, Tit-for-Tat (cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move), Generous Tit-for-Tat (forgives 10% of betrayals), and Pavlov (cooperate if both made the same move last round, otherwise defect).

Each generation, everyone plays 6 random opponents for a set number of rounds each. Mutual cooperation scores 3, mutual defection 1, defecting against a cooperator earns the "temptation" score (5 by default), and cooperating against a defector scores 0.
Occasionally a move flips by mistake. A slider sets the chance of a mistake.
